items.title: The brain benefits of letting children do things on their own
items.summary: Giving children more freedom feels risky, but research on independent play has motivated me to let my daughter go, says columnist Helen Thomson
items.t: The brain benefits of letting children do things on their own

items.title: Motion under the ocean explains the depth of the world’s deepest spot
items.summary: The deepest known remnants of explosive volcanism offer a new clue to how Challenger Deep became the ocean's deepest point.
items.t: Motion under the ocean explains the depth of the world’s deepest spot

items.title: Common medications may secretly rewire your gut, with effects lasting for years
items.summary: Medications taken years or even long ago may leave lasting changes in your gut microbiome, according to a study of more than 2,500 people. Researchers discovered that common drugs, including antidepressants, blood pressure medications, and anxiety treatments, can leave microbial “fingerprints” long after patients stop taking them. Surprisingly, some anxiety medications had effects comparable to broad-spectrum antibiotics.
items.t: Common medications may secretly rewire your gut, with effects lasting for years

items.title: Interstellar solar sails hit a bizarre problem at 75% of light speed
items.summary: Scientists have discovered a surprising obstacle to interstellar travel: at extreme speeds, the light propelling futuristic solar sails could actually begin slowing them down. Once a spacecraft reaches 75% of the speed of light, some scattered light starts producing drag, potentially complicating humanity’s plans to reach distant stars.
items.t: Interstellar solar sails hit a bizarre problem at 75% of light speed

items.title: A mysterious gap hints at black holes born from stars that never exploded
items.summary: Massive stars may be quietly collapsing into black holes without ever producing the spectacular supernova explosions scientists typically expect. A surprising pattern in 257 black hole mergers suggests these mysterious stellar disappearances could explain the origins of a large population of black holes throughout the universe.
items.t: A mysterious gap hints at black holes born from stars that never exploded

items.title: DNA’s secret sunscreen may have helped life survive on early Earth
items.summary: Scientists have uncovered a surprising reason why early life may have survived Earth's intense ultraviolet radiation: a key component of DNA appears to turn potentially destructive damage into something easier to repair. The discovery could help solve a decades-old evolutionary mystery and reveal how life endured the harsh conditions of our planet's earliest days.
items.t: DNA’s secret sunscreen may have helped life survive on early Earth

items.title: A 194-year-old tortoise has a remarkable anti-aging secret hidden in its DNA
items.summary: At an astonishing 194 years old, Jonathan the giant tortoise is the world's oldest living land animal, and scientists may have finally uncovered the secrets behind his extraordinary lifespan. Researchers identified 287 unique genetic variants linked to processes that help repair damaged DNA, control inflammation, regulate insulin, and suppress cancer.
items.t: A 194-year-old tortoise has a remarkable anti-aging secret hidden in its DNA

items.title: Time may be far stranger than we realize. Scientists have a way to test it
items.summary: Time may be far stranger than we realize, and scientists have proposed a way to detect clocks experiencing multiple flows of time simultaneously. Using atomic clocks with dramatically enhanced sensitivity, researchers hope to reveal a never-before-observed quantum effect that could transform our understanding of time and gravity.
items.t: Time may be far stranger than we realize. Scientists have a way to test it

items.title: A giant star swallowed another star. James Webb reveals the aftermath
items.summary: Astronomers have witnessed a spectacular cosmic collision in the Andromeda galaxy, where a small star spiraled into a giant star 18,000 times brighter than the Sun, triggering a violent eruption. NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope captured the aftermath just 47 days later, revealing new details about how two stars can merge into one.
items.t: A giant star swallowed another star. James Webb reveals the aftermath

items.title: Who was buried in Westminster Abbey's Roman coffin? A 150-year mystery may be solved
items.summary: A mysterious skeleton discovered in a Roman sarcophagus at Westminster Abbey may finally be identified after more than 150 years. New dating evidence suggests the remains belonged to a high-ranking medieval abbot who was buried inside a centuries-old recycled Roman coffin.
items.t: Who was buried in Westminster Abbey's Roman coffin? A 150-year mystery may be solved

items.title: A 50-year-old theory about evolution may have been wrong all along
items.summary: A decades-old theory suggesting that evolution protects its most important genes from mutations has been dealt a major blow. An extensive new analysis of mutations in bacteria and yeast found no evidence that essential genes mutate less frequently than other genes. Researchers say earlier studies may have been misled by harmful mutations that disappeared through natural selection before scientists could detect them.
items.t: A 50-year-old theory about evolution may have been wrong all along

items.title: Even scientists can't agree on what science actually is
items.summary: Scientists cannot agree on what science actually is, and a new study finds their views are surprisingly more divided than those of the general public. The findings could help explain public frustration with scientific uncertainty and raise questions about how artificial intelligence might reshape future discoveries.
items.t: Even scientists can't agree on what science actually is

items.title: Scientists say the human family tree may need a radical rewrite
items.summary: The human family tree may need a major overhaul. New research from Monash University challenges the traditional classification of our ancient ancestors, arguing that species such as Australopithecus and Paranthropus should be grouped within our own genus, Homo. As scientists uncover more fossils and analyze evolutionary relationships, the boundaries that once separated these ancient relatives are becoming increasingly difficult to defend.
items.t: Scientists say the human family tree may need a radical rewrite

items.title: Astronomer Isabel Angelo hunts for odd signals in telescope data
items.summary: At the SETI Institute, she uses machine learning to look for signs of cosmic phenomena astronomers have never seen before.
items.t: Astronomer Isabel Angelo hunts for odd signals in telescope data

items.title: This scientist proves which problems computers can’t solve quickly
items.summary: Dor Minzer studies how fast computers can tell whether nearly all of a game’s rules can be satisfied or almost none can.
items.t: This scientist proves which problems computers can’t solve quickly

items.title: What helps land recover after fire? This ecologist looks to the past
items.summary: Ecologist Jennifer Grenz draws on Indigenous oral histories and ecological records to learn how landscapes recover after wildfires.
items.t: What helps land recover after fire? This ecologist looks to the past

items.title: How do scientists learn from failure? This researcher has clues
items.summary: Yian Yin found that scientists who revised rejected proposals using feedback found success faster than those who switched ideas.
items.t: How do scientists learn from failure? This researcher has clues

items.title: How do tumors talk to nerves? This scientist is finding out
items.summary: After finding proteins linked to memory in prostate cancer cells, Sebnem Ece Eksi hopes to map nerve fibers in tumors.
items.t: How do tumors talk to nerves? This scientist is finding out

items.title: After 8 years in space, a groundbreaking X-ray telescope finally opens its eyes
items.summary: After eight years and 10 billion kilometers in space, a groundbreaking X-ray telescope heading to Mercury has captured its first cosmic observations and is performing even better than scientists expected. The instrument could soon reveal Mercury's hidden chemical secrets and transform our understanding of how the solar system's smallest planet formed.
items.t: After 8 years in space, a groundbreaking X-ray telescope finally opens its eyes

items.title: Mathematicians are amazed by ‘holy grail’ proof of Riemann hypothesis
items.summary: As news spread that an Anthropic researcher used AI to find an answer to one of the longest-standing questions in their field, mathematicians expressed awe, uncertainty and at least one claim of having a competing proof in the works
items.t: Mathematicians are amazed by ‘holy grail’ proof of Riemann hypothesis

items.title: Quantum effect could reverse gravity and violate Einstein’s theory of relativity
items.summary: Two mathematical investigations devised a way to possibly make gravity produce repulsion between objects, breaking away from a long-standing understanding of this force
items.t: Quantum effect could reverse gravity and violate Einstein’s theory of relativity

items.title: What is the Riemann hypothesis and why is its solution so monumental?
items.summary:
Bernhard Riemann set out a problem mathematicians have been trying solve for more than a century The Granger Collection/Alamy 

The cadence of prime numbers has a pattern; it isn’t simply chaos. Mathematician Bernhard Riemann suspected this was the case, but he never proved it conclusively, and his mathematical successors have spent more than a century trying to demonstrate that he was right. The Riemann hypothesis may now be proven , and it could reveal the most basic structure of our number system, while also opening the door for a new understanding of the vast world of mathematical functions.

Read more 
 Mathematicians and AI in behind-the-scenes battle over what’s true

In 1859, Riemann made a casual remark about a mathematical function in his memoir, qualifying a statement about it as “very probably” true. The fact that he never proved it more definitively has held the world of mathematics in suspense ever since, and the “Riemann hypothesis” became the field’s most famous and stubbornly unsolved problem – until now. A new AI-assisted proof by Levent Alpöge at Anthropic may have just ended a whole era of mathematics by confirming Riemann’s hunch from nearly 200 years ago.

“This result, if true, will be the culmination of a struggle thousands of mathematicians have attempted in the past,” says Christopher Hughes at the University of York in the UK. items.title: Anthropic mathematician claims AI-assisted proof of the Riemann hypothesis
items.summary:
The Riemann hypothesis describes a pattern within the prime numbers ROBERT BROOK/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY/Alamy 

A mathematician at AI company Anthropic claims to have discovered, and verified with formalisation, a proof of the Riemann hypothesis – one of the most infamous and thorny problems in all of mathematics.

The Riemann hypothesis was first put forward in 1859 by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann. It proposes an origin for the prime numbers, namely that they follow a certain pattern. The question is one of the Clay Mathematics Institute Millennium Prize Problems, which will award a $1 million prize for an accepted solution.

Read more 
 OpenAI has dumped 722 maths papers – now it must clean up the mess

Levent Alpöge at Anthropic published a statement today claiming to have solved the problem with the aid of Anthropic’s Claude AI. 

Advertisement 

“I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann hypothesis,” writes Alpöge. “It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater.” In August, Anthropic announced previous work on the Riemann hypothesis , but that stopped short of a full proof.

Alpöge hasn’t published a human-readable version of the proof, saying it would be “obviously inappropriate to attempt to post some massive unreadable travesty of ‘slop'”, though he says an unpublished version ran to more than 250,000 pages.

items.summary:
One evening in the fall of 1969, a team of researchers sent a historic message from a computer in Los Angeles to one in Menlo Park, California. Or rather, they sent part of the message: the “L” and “O” in “LOGIN.” The first transmission over the first link in Arpanet, the prototype for the modern internet, lasted all of two characters before the network crashed. Computer networks have grown much…

items.summary: More than 70 countries are ready to begin negotiations on prohibiting lethal autonomous weapons, but large militarised nations are expected to obstruct efforts to agree a ban
items.t: US, Russia and China look set to block ban on autonomous weapons

items.title: A fast-growing heart is good for the Grinch. People are another story
items.summary: In the classic Dr. Seuss tale, the rapid growth signals an emotional change of heart. In real life, a swollen heart can be a sign of stress or disease.
items.t: A fast-growing heart is good for the Grinch. People are another story

items.title: Einstein’s relativity just upended a fundamental rule of chemistry
items.summary: A surprising discovery at Brown University is challenging one of chemistry's most fundamental textbook explanations. Researchers found direct evidence that Einstein's theory of relativity changes how heavy atoms form triple bonds, causing normally distinct types of chemical bonds to blend together. The breakthrough confirms a decades-old prediction and suggests that traditional chemistry rules don't fully apply to heavy elements such as bismuth.
items.t: Einstein’s relativity just upended a fundamental rule of chemistry

items.title: NASA’s Voyager 1 is now so far away that light takes 24 hours to reach it
items.summary: NASA’s Voyager 1 has reached an extraordinary milestone, traveling 16.1 billion miles from Earth to become the first spacecraft so distant that its signals take a full day to reach us. Nearly 50 years after launch, the aging probe continues its historic journey through interstellar space, pushing the limits of human exploration despite dwindling power and technical challenges.
items.t: NASA’s Voyager 1 is now so far away that light takes 24 hours to reach it

items.title: Scientists turn Moon dust into LEGO-like bricks for future lunar bases
items.summary: Scientists have found a way to 3D-print Moon dust into LEGO-like bricks, raising the possibility of building lunar bases using materials already on the Moon. The experimental blocks still need to be strengthened, but the technology could transform how humans construct permanent settlements beyond Earth.
items.t: Scientists turn Moon dust into LEGO-like bricks for future lunar bases

items.title: CERN scientists finally find evidence of a particle decay so rare it took 40 years to detect
items.summary: Scientists at CERN have found the first evidence of an incredibly rare particle decay after more than 40 years of searching, detecting a process expected to occur just once in every 10 billion beauty particles. The breakthrough could help physicists explore a mysterious microscopic realm where unknown particles and forces may be hiding.
items.t: CERN scientists finally find evidence of a particle decay so rare it took 40 years to detect

items.title: Unexpected stone tools from Israel raise questions about cultural evolution
items.summary: Ancient humans in the eastern Mediterranean first began producing advanced stone blades 100,000 years before the tools became widely used, indicating that new technologies weren't automatically adopted by communities
items.t: Unexpected stone tools from Israel raise questions about cultural evolution

items.title: Dark Eden author Chris Beckett on how sci-fi needs ‘surface plausibility’
items.summary:
Dark Eden , the November read for the New Scientist Book Club, is set on a planet drifting alone outside the Milky Way, where the descendants of two astronauts struggle to survive. Author Chris Beckett talked to Alison Flood about how he dreamed up the flora and fauna on this sunless world, how the genetics of this community work – and how, once he’d built his alien world, he set about telling his story.

items.title: The secret maths problems hidden throughout Japan
items.summary: Hundreds of years ago, Japanese mathematicians enshrined their work onto painted wooden tablets displayed throughout the country. Columnist Jacob Aron explores the history of the practice of sangaku and the effort to digitally preserve these artefacts
items.t: The secret maths problems hidden throughout Japan

items.title: Two massive stars may be secretly feeding the Milky Way’s supermassive black hole
items.summary: Astronomers have traced mysterious gas clouds near the Milky Way's central supermassive black hole to a massive pair of stars whose colliding winds appear to create dense clumps of material. These clouds may eventually feed the black hole, revealing a surprising connection between stellar activity and the growth of cosmic giants.
items.t: Two massive stars may be secretly feeding the Milky Way’s supermassive black hole

items.title: A 3-million-year-old child just made human evolution far more complicated
items.summary: A groundbreaking study of the 3-million-year-old Taung Child fossil suggests that several ancient human ancestors once thought to belong to the same species may actually represent different branches of our evolutionary family tree. The discovery challenges a century of assumptions and reveals how dramatic climate changes helped shape a surprisingly complex story of human origins.
items.t: A 3-million-year-old child just made human evolution far more complicated

items.title: Experimental compound burns fat without sacrificing muscle
items.summary: Researchers at UC Berkeley have identified a compound that could transform weight-loss treatment by helping the body burn more energy instead of suppressing appetite like Ozempic and Wegovy. In mice, the compound boosted energy expenditure by up to 18%, improved blood sugar control, reduced liver fat, and promoted weight loss without significant muscle loss. Even more promising, combining it with existing GLP-1 medications produced greater benefits than either treatment alone.
items.t: Experimental compound burns fat without sacrificing muscle

items.title: Solo meerkats can find their way back home
items.summary: Meerkats wearing GPS trackers found their way home from more than a kilometer away, all by themselves.
items.t: Solo meerkats can find their way back home

items.title: A brain region known for listening helps us speak
items.summary: Recording Wernicke’s area as people try to speak could help researchers design brain implants that restore speech.
items.t: A brain region known for listening helps us speak

items.title: U.S. demand for menopause hormone therapy has more than doubled recently
items.summary: The use of menopause hormone therapy among women aged 40 to 74 rose from 2023 to 2026, suggests a study of a U.S. pharmacy database.
items.t: U.S. demand for menopause hormone therapy has more than doubled recently

items.title: American science is broken. Meet the people fixing it
items.summary: After a massive realignment of U.S. science priorities last year, researchers are rebuilding — and reimagining — what has been broken.
items.t: American science is broken. Meet the people fixing it

items.title: Scientists tested 212 plant-based foods. Every single one contained fungal toxins
items.summary: A new study has uncovered a surprising concern hiding in popular plant-based foods and drinks. Researchers tested 212 vegan and vegetarian products sold in the UK, including meat alternatives, oat milk, almond milk, and soy milk, and found that every single one contained at least one potentially harmful fungal toxin. Known as mycotoxins, these naturally occurring compounds can contaminate grains, legumes, and seeds during farming and storage.
items.t: Scientists tested 212 plant-based foods. Every single one contained fungal toxins

items.title: This 6-million-year-old whale may have had the most crooked face in mammal history
items.summary: A bizarre whale that lived roughly 6 million years ago had a face so dramatically crooked that scientists believe it may have been the most asymmetrical of any mammal. Discovered in Peru, the extinct pygmy sperm whale Scaphokogia huachafo had an enormous downward-curving snout and a skull so distorted that researchers initially thought it had been damaged after death. Instead, its strange anatomy appears to have been an extraordinary evolutionary adaptation for hunting along the seafloor.
items.t: This 6-million-year-old whale may have had the most crooked face in mammal history

items.title: Something strange is living beneath the skin of deep-sea pigs
items.summary: Scientists have discovered a strange bacterium hiding beneath the skin of deep-sea creatures known as sea pigs, revealing an unexpected biological partnership. The microbe has an unusually tiny genome, yet more than a quarter of its DNA is devoted to making surface proteins, some of them exceptionally large. Researchers suspect it depends heavily on its host for survival, but what the sea pigs gain in return remains a mystery.
items.t: Something strange is living beneath the skin of deep-sea pigs

items.title: Why hydrogen flames can glow orange, then turn nearly invisible
items.summary: Hydrogen flames can shift from bright orange to nearly invisible depending on something unexpected: tiny amounts of sodium floating in the air. Scientists say this discovery could help make future hydrogen-powered stoves and ovens safer by replacing visual flame detection with specialized sensors.
items.t: Why hydrogen flames can glow orange, then turn nearly invisible

items.title: Is free will an illusion? New brain research reveals a surprising twist
items.summary: New research reveals that the brain makes free choices and forced decisions using surprisingly similar neural processes, with activity building toward a decision before we act. The discovery challenges assumptions about free will while suggesting that our personal preferences and experiences still shape what we choose.
items.t: Is free will an illusion? New brain research reveals a surprising twist

items.summary: Launched in 1977, Voyager 1 has traveled farther than any other human-made object.

items.title: How M.C. Escher’s Art Creates Bizarre Mathematical Worlds
items.summary:
Maurits Cornelis Escher didn’t plan on becoming the darling of mathematicians. Born in 1898 in the canal-lined city of Leeuwarden in the Netherlands, Escher struggled with mathematics as a student, once remarking that he “never got a pass mark.” He ended up studying decorative arts and printmaking, and he used his artwork to explore the strange rules of nature that he found operating around him.

Source

items.title: Why do farts smell so bad? The secret is brewing in your gut
items.summary: The secret behind truly terrible-smelling farts lies in tiny amounts of sulfur-containing gases produced by gut bacteria as they digest food. Scientists reveal why some foods make farts smell worse, why loud farts aren't always the stinkiest, and how our noses evolved to detect these powerful odors.
